Verifiable rewards

Lesson 91's problem came from a learned reward model that is wrong away from its data. For maths and code there is another option: a program checks the final answer and pays 1 if it is right, 0 if not. This is reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). It is much harder to game, but only if the checker is written carefully, and the reward is sparse.

Learning from 0s and 1s

30 problems of increasing difficulty $d_j$. The model's chance of solving problem $j$ is $p_j = \sigma(\theta - d_j)$, where $\theta$ is its skill and $\sigma$ the logistic function. Each training step samples one answer per problem, the verifier pays $r_j \in \{0, 1\}$, and REINFORCE (Lesson 73) updates $\theta$. Green: $p_j$. Purple tick: the learning signal $p_j(1-p_j)$, scaled so 0.25 is the top.

Try $\theta_0 = -5$: almost every reward is 0, so $\theta$ barely moves for hundreds of steps, then takes off once the easiest problems start paying. At $\theta_0 = -8$ it hardly moves at all.

The maths

For a prompt $x$ with known answer $y^\star$ and a sampled response $y$, the verifiable reward is

$$r(x, y) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{answer in } y = y^\star \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$

The checker is code, not a network, so it does not drift or extrapolate. But it is still a proxy for "solved the problem". The extraction rule is part of the reward, and any gap in it (like "contains a 7") is a gap the policy can learn to exploit, exactly as in Lesson 90.

With $p = \Pr(r = 1)$ the expected reward is just the pass rate, and the reward's variance is that of a coin flip:

$$\mathbb{E}[r] = p, \qquad \operatorname{Var}(r) = p(1 - p)$$

In the toy model, $\pi_\theta$ answers problem $j$ correctly with probability $p_j = \sigma(\theta - d_j)$. Then $\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(r_j) = r_j - p_j$ and the REINFORCE gradient is

$$\mathbb{E}\big[r_j \,(r_j - p_j)\big] = p_j (1 - p_j)$$

Problems the model always fails ($p \approx 0$) or always solves ($p \approx 1$) teach it nothing. Learning happens on problems at the edge of its ability.

Sampling $k$ answers per problem helps on hard problems: the chance that at least one is right is

$$\text{pass@}k = 1 - (1 - p)^k$$

Tülu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024) trained with verifiable rewards on maths problems with known answers and on instructions with checkable constraints ("answer in under 50 words").
